6.text: The adult body synthesizes ≈ 1 g of cholesterol a day (mainly in the liver) and takes in 0.3–0.5 g with food. The steran ring is not broken down in the body: cholesterol is excreted with bile into the intestine mainly as **bile acids** and unchanged; ≈ 95 % of bile acids are reabsorbed in the terminal small intestine and return to the liver (**enterohepatic circulation**).

Cells take up LDL by endocytosis through special **LDL receptors**. When cholesterol in the cell increases, the synthesis of HMG-CoA reductase and the number of receptors decrease — this is **negative feedback**. Statins reduce cellular cholesterol and increase the number of LDL receptors in the liver — more LDL is taken up from the blood.

parts.text: **Familial hypercholesterolemia** is a mutation of the LDL receptor gene: LDL is not removed from the blood and its cholesterol rises sharply (5–10 in heterozygotes, > 13 mmol/L in homozygotes). **Xanthomas** in tendons, xanthelasmas around the eyes and myocardial infarction at a young age (in homozygotes even in childhood) develop. Treatment: statins, ezetimibe (blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption), PCSK9 inhibitors.

blocks.text: Because fats are insoluble in water, their digestion and transport require special mechanisms. In the small intestine **bile acids** emulsify fats, and pancreatic **lipase** (with the help of colipase) breaks triglycerides down into 2-monoacylglycerol and fatty acids. The digestion products form **mixed micelles** with bile acids and reach the enterocytes; there triglycerides are resynthesized and released into the lymph in **chylomicrons**.

In the blood lipids are transported as **lipoproteins**: in the center of the spherical particle are the nonpolar triglycerides and cholesterol esters, and on the surface are phospholipids, free cholesterol and proteins — **apolipoproteins**. The greater the lipid fraction, the lower the density.

blocks.text: **Lipoprotein lipase** on the vascular endothelium (activated by apo C-II) breaks down the triglycerides of chylomicrons and VLDL; the fatty acids pass into muscle and adipose tissue, and VLDL is gradually converted into LDL. LDL enters the vessel wall and is oxidized; macrophages engulf it and become “foam cells” — the beginning of an **atherosclerotic plaque**.

parts.text: LDL cholesterol is often calculated with the **Friedewald formula** (in mmol/L): LDL = total cholesterol − HDL − triglycerides / 2.2 (when triglycerides < 4.5 mmol/L). **Atherogenic index** = (total cholesterol − HDL) / HDL; normally less than 3.

blocks.text: **Eicosanoids** are locally acting hormone-like substances formed from 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acids, mainly **arachidonic acid**. Arachidonic acid is released from membrane phospholipids by **phospholipase A~2~** and is then converted by two pathways.

parts.text: **ω-3 fatty acids** (EPA, DHA) are also substrates of COX and lipoxygenase, but the eicosanoids formed from them stimulate inflammation and thrombus formation more weakly. This is how a fish-rich diet is linked to a lower risk of cardiovascular disease.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: A patient’s lipid profile: total cholesterol 6.6 mmol/L, HDL cholesterol 1.1 mmol/L, triglycerides 3.3 mmol/L.
cases.ask: Calculate and assess the LDL cholesterol and the atherogenic index.
cases.answer: LDL = 6.6 − 1.1 − 3.3 / 2.2 = 6.6 − 1.1 − 1.5 = **4.0 mmol/L** (normal < 3.0 — raised). AI = (6.6 − 1.1) / 1.1 = **5** (normal < 3). Total cholesterol and triglycerides are also raised — **atherogenic dyslipidemia**, high cardiovascular risk. Diet, physical activity and statin treatment are considered.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: A 12-year-old child has yellowish nodules (xanthomas) on the elbow and Achilles tendons. His father died of a myocardial infarction at the age of 38. The child’s LDL cholesterol is 14 mmol/L, and triglycerides are normal.
cases.ask: Which disease is suspected? Explain its molecular cause and the principle of treatment.
cases.answer: This is **familial hypercholesterolemia**; the very high LDL and xanthomas in childhood are typical of the **homozygous** form. Because of a defect in the **LDL receptor**, the liver and other cells cannot take up LDL from the blood; with too little cholesterol inside the cell, HMG-CoA reductase stays active and cholesterol synthesis does not stop. Excess LDL accumulates in the tissues (xanthomas) and in the vessel wall, leading to early atherosclerosis. Treatment: high-dose statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, and in severe cases LDL apheresis (removing LDL from the blood).

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A patient with chronic pancreatitis has bulky, fatty, shiny, foul-smelling stools that are hard to flush. When the stool was stained with Sudan III, many orange-red droplets were seen.
cases.ask: What is the condition? What is its biochemical cause and how is it treated?
cases.answer: This is **steatorrhea** — excretion of a lot of fat in the stool (Sudan III stains neutral fat droplets). In chronic pancreatitis the production of pancreatic **lipase** and colipase decreases — triglycerides are not broken down and not absorbed. As a result, the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are also deficient. Treatment: **enzyme preparations** (pancreatin) taken with meals, a moderate fat intake, and supplements of fat-soluble vitamins.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A 65-year-old patient who took diclofenac every day for a month for knee osteoarthritis developed black stools and weakness; endoscopy revealed a gastric ulcer.
cases.ask: Explain the formation of the ulcer in terms of eicosanoid metabolism. How could the risk have been reduced?
cases.answer: Diclofenac is a nonselective **COX inhibitor**. In the gastric mucosa **PGE~2~** and prostacyclin formed by COX-1 increase mucus and bicarbonate secretion, improve blood flow and reduce HCl secretion — that is, they protect the mucosa. When COX is blocked, this protection is lost and acid erodes the mucosa — ulcer and bleeding (black stool — melena). Ways to reduce the risk: the lowest effective dose for a short time, giving a proton pump inhibitor at the same time, and, if possible, a selective COX-2 inhibitor or paracetamol.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A woman with bronchial asthma and nasal polyps took aspirin for a headache and 30 minutes later had a severe attack of breathlessness.
cases.ask: Why did aspirin trigger an asthma attack? Which drug group is especially useful for such patients?
cases.answer: This is **aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease**. When aspirin blocks cyclooxygenase, arachidonic acid is not used in the COX pathway and is “shunted” to the **lipoxygenase** pathway — much bronchoconstricting **leukotrienes** (LTC~4~, LTD~4~) are formed; in addition, the bronchoprotective PGE~2~ decreases. The result is severe bronchospasm. Such patients are not given aspirin or other nonselective NSAIDs; **leukotriene receptor antagonists** (montelukast) and inhaled glucocorticoids are useful in treatment.
